strengths: Addresses a useful problem: controllable, class-agnostic 3D part segmentation with both interactive and automatic inference. The combination of a promptable decoder, triplane features, and large-scale supervision is technically plausible and practically relevant.

Reports substantial interactive improvements over Point-SAM on two benchmarks. Single-click IoU increases from 29.4 to 56.1 on PartObjaverse-Tiny and from 35.9 to 59.5 on PartNetE, with gains persisting across additional clicks.
The data pipeline scales to approximately 500,000 shapes and five million parts. Table 3 provides positive evidence that both the dual-branch encoder and expanded training corpus improve performance.

Qualitative examples show promising segmentation of detailed artist-created and generated meshes. Reported automatic inference takes approximately 12 seconds, substantially faster than the evaluated per-shape optimization methods.
weaknesses: The automatic-segmentation comparison overstates the advantage over PartField. The main table replaces its connectivity-aware clustering with K-Means, reducing its PartObjaverse-Tiny IoU to 51.5. Appendix Table 4 reports 79.2 for standard PartField and 81.3 for PartSAM with connectivity, a much smaller advantage. Connectivity available in the input is not inherently ground-truth leakage; these are different evaluation settings, and both should be prominent. Retaining connectivity for SAMesh further complicates the main comparison.

The claimed open-world generalization is insufficiently established. Training draws from Objaverse and PartNet, while evaluation uses PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE, but the manuscript does not document asset-level exclusions, duplicate removal, or category-disjoint splits. This does not establish contamination, but it leaves a central uncertainty about whether the reported gains reflect generalization to genuinely unseen shapes.

The data contribution lacks an independent quality assessment. Agreement with PartField pseudo-labels after simulated corrective clicks measures reproducibility of those labels, not necessarily semantic correctness. There is no human audit, annotation precision estimate, or size-matched comparison against unfiltered pseudo-labels. The data ablation therefore conflates filtering quality with additional training volume.

Novelty and causal claims need sharper support. Much of the architecture combines PartField features with SAM-style decoding and a frozen/trainable branch design. The ablations do not isolate additional normals/RGB, branch capacity, pretraining, or the triplet loss. Claims about catastrophic forgetting and superior scalability are not directly tested. Moreover, both encoder initialization and expanded pseudo-labels depend on SAM-derived PartField knowledge, so the framing of native 3D learning as an alternative to transferring 2D priors is overstated.

Evaluation does not substantiate several headline capabilities. Interior-part segmentation and robustness on generated meshes are demonstrated qualitatively rather than through dedicated quantitative tests. Automatic evaluation selects the best matching masks across multiple granularities, which does not establish the quality of a single deployable decomposition or penalize redundant proposals adequately. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

Important reproducibility details are missing or inconsistent: the automatic prompt count, predicted-IoU filtering threshold, overlap/uncovered-face assignment, and IoU-head training objective are unspecified. Appendix A.1 describes initial prompts near the background, whereas the main text describes central prompts. Table 3 also reports different full-model results from Tables 1–2 without explanation. Code and weights are only promised, and the curated dataset's release status is unclear.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: promptable, class-agnostic 3D part segmentation with both interactive and automatic inference.

Reports substantial interactive improvements over Point-SAM on two benchmarks. Single-click IoU increases from 29.4 to 56.1 on PartObjaverse-Tiny and from 35.9 to 59.5 on PartNetE, with improvements persisting across additional clicks.

The large-scale data pipeline and dual-branch encoder form a useful engineering contribution. Table 3 provides positive evidence for the encoder design and expanded training corpus, including a Point-SAM encoder comparison under matched training settings.

Qualitative results demonstrate promising segmentation of complex and generated assets. Reported automatic inference takes approximately 12 seconds per shape, substantially faster than the optimization-based baselines.
weaknesses: The main automatic-segmentation comparison weakens the strongest baseline by replacing PartField's connectivity-aware clustering with K-Means. Connectivity available in the input mesh is not inherently ground-truth leakage, and SAMesh retains access to it. Appendix Table 4 shows standard connectivity-enabled PartField achieving 79.2 IoU, versus 69.5 for the main PartSAM configuration; adding connectivity post-processing to PartSAM yields 81.3. This is a useful improvement, but substantially less decisive than the headline comparison suggests. Both matched settings should be prominent.

The open-world generalization claim lacks a documented contamination audit. Training uses Objaverse assets and PartNet labels, while evaluation uses PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE. The manuscript does not specify benchmark exclusions, asset-level deduplication, or category-disjoint splits. This does not establish contamination, but leaves a central claim insufficiently supported.

The automatic evaluation selects the best-overlapping candidate masks across segmentation scales. This measures oracle candidate coverage rather than the quality of a single automatically selected decomposition. It does not adequately establish complete, coherent segmentation with appropriate granularity, coverage, and non-overlapping parts. Candidate budgets and matching details also need clarification.

The distinctive interior-structure and generated-mesh claims are supported primarily by selected visual examples. There is no dedicated quantitative interior-part evaluation or annotated generated-mesh benchmark. The amodal examples additionally depend on HoloPart, so they do not independently establish PartSAM's completion capabilities.

The methodological novelty is mostly the integration of established components: PartField features, a SAM-style decoder, a frozen/trainable branch design, and prompt sampling with NMS. The native-3D framing needs qualification because both branches inherit PartField's SAM-derived priors and the expanded corpus uses PartField pseudo-labels. The ablations do not isolate extra capacity, normals/RGB, the triplet loss, or annotation filtering from increased data volume; consequently, claims about scalability and catastrophic forgetting exceed the demonstrated evidence.

Dataset quality and reproducibility remain insufficiently established for a contribution centered on five million annotations. Agreement between related models does not independently verify semantic label quality, and no human audit or quantitative annotation-quality analysis is provided. Important details—including automatic prompt count, confidence threshold, IoU-head supervision, and overlap/uncovered-region handling—are unspecified. Results also differ without explanation between Tables 1–3, including automatic IoU of 69.5 versus 68.5. Code and model release is promised, but dataset availability is unclear.

strengths: PartSAM addresses a meaningful problem: combining interactive and automatic 3D part segmentation with supervision that includes interior geometry. The integration of a promptable decoder, dual-branch triplane encoder, and large-scale annotation pipeline is practically compelling.

Interactive results are strong on both benchmarks. Single-click IoU improves from 29.4 to 56.1 on PartObjaverse-Tiny and from 35.9 to 59.5 on PartNetE, with substantial gains persisting through ten prompts.

The ablations provide useful evidence for the proposed components: the full model outperforms the Point-SAM encoder, frozen and trainable PartField encoders, and training without model-in-the-loop annotations.

Automatic segmentation compares against several relevant methods. The appendix also reports a positive result with mesh connectivity enabled for both approaches: 81.3 IoU versus PartField's 79.2. Reported inference takes approximately 12 seconds per shape, substantially faster than lifting-based alternatives.
weaknesses: The open-world evaluation lacks an explicit training/test exclusion and deduplication protocol. Training uses Objaverse and PartNet, while evaluation uses PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE. This does not establish contamination, but asset-level overlap checks and clear held-out splits are necessary to substantiate the central generalization claims.

The headline automatic-segmentation gains depend substantially on modifying PartField to remove connectivity and use K-Means. Useful connectivity in an input mesh is not inherently ground-truth leakage. The appendix's comparison with connectivity enabled reduces the advantage to 2.1 IoU points; this more competitive result should be central to the discussion. Removing connectivity and changing clustering also confounds two factors.

Automatic evaluation reports the best IoU across candidate masks and segmentation scales. This measures oracle proposal quality rather than fully autonomous decomposition, and does not adequately penalize redundant or inconsistent predictions. Results with a fixed selection policy, matched proposal budgets, and partition or precision-sensitive metrics are needed.

Several central claims exceed the evidence. Interior segmentation and robustness to generated meshes are demonstrated qualitatively without dedicated quantitative evaluation. Scalability is inferred from endpoint comparisons rather than scaling curves, and the catastrophic-forgetting explanation lacks direct measurement. Architectural comparisons also do not isolate additional capacity, input attributes, and preserved pretrained features.

The dataset contribution needs stronger validation. Agreement between PartSAM and PartField pseudo-labels is not independent evidence of semantic correctness, especially after corrective prompts target those labels. There is no quantitative annotation-quality audit or controlled comparison against unfiltered pseudo-labels. Moreover, both pretrained encoders and the expanded annotations depend on SAM-derived PartField knowledge, qualifying the contrast with 2D-supervised approaches.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: automatic prompt count, confidence threshold, overlap/uncovered-point handling, and IoU-head training details are insufficiently specified. Dataset access is unclear, and code/model release is only promised. Tables 1 and 3 also report different multi-click results for the full model, while automatic IoU differs between Tables 2 and 3 without explanation.

strengths: PartSAM addresses a meaningful problem: combining interactive and automatic 3D part segmentation with supervision that includes interior geometry. The integration of a promptable decoder, dual-branch triplane encoder, and large-scale data curation is practically compelling.

Interactive results are strong: single-click IoU improves from 29.4 to 56.1 on PartObjaverse-Tiny and from 35.9 to 59.5 on PartNetE. Retraining Point-SAM on the proposed data provides useful evidence that data scale alone does not explain the gains.

The appendix provides substantial supporting experiments, including encoder and data ablations, scaling curves, runtime measurements, connectivity-aware comparisons, and additional evaluation on five 3DCoMPaT++ categories.

Qualitative results demonstrate promising segmentation of occluded structures and generated meshes. Reported automatic inference takes approximately 12 seconds per shape, substantially faster than the optimization-based baselines.
weaknesses: Training–test independence is insufficiently documented. Training includes Objaverse(-XL) and PartNet assets, while evaluation uses PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE, but no explicit exclusion lists, asset-level deduplication procedure, or held-out category protocol are provided. This leaves the central open-world generalization claim difficult to verify; it does not establish that contamination occurred.

The headline automatic-segmentation comparison weakens PartField by removing connectivity and replacing its clustering with K-means. Connectivity being predictive of artist-defined parts does not itself constitute ground-truth leakage. The appendix usefully supplies connectivity-aware results, but the advantage there is only 81.3 versus 79.2 IoU, substantially qualifying the claimed large-margin superiority.

Automatic evaluation selects the best IoU across candidate masks and segmentation scales. Although applied to baselines as well, this oracle protocol does not establish the quality of a single automatically selected decomposition and can depend on proposal count. Fixed-setting results, explicit mask-matching rules, and coverage or oversegmentation metrics are needed.

The annotation pipeline measures agreement between PartSAM and PartField rather than independently verified semantic correctness. No quantitative annotation audit supports the assertion that erroneous labels are negligible. Moreover, both encoder initialization and second-stage pseudo-labels inherit SAM-derived information, making the categorical contrast with 2D-supervised approaches too strong.

Architectural novelty is primarily an integration of existing components. The ablations do not separately isolate auxiliary input attributes, the triplet loss, and the additional encoder capacity, so explanations based on avoiding catastrophic forgetting or superior architectural scalability remain only partially supported. Interior segmentation is also demonstrated qualitatively without a dedicated quantitative benchmark.

Reproducibility needs improvement: exact data manifests, filtering thresholds, confidence thresholds, and rules for resolving overlapping or uncovered automatic masks are missing. Tables 1–3 report inconsistent full-model results without explanation, and uncertainty estimates are absent, which matters particularly for the smaller connectivity-aware improvement.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: controllable, open-world 3D part segmentation, including occluded structures. Combining interactive segmentation and automatic decomposition is practically useful.
Reported interactive improvements are substantial: single-click IoU increases from 29.4 to 56.1 on PartObjaverse-Tiny and from 35.9 to 59.5 on PartNetE relative to Point-SAM.

The evaluation includes meaningful supporting experiments: Point-SAM retrained on the proposed dataset, encoder and training-data ablations, data-scaling curves, runtime measurements, and additional 3DCoMPaT++ results.

The automated curation pipeline reaches an impressive scale of 500,000 shapes and over five million parts. The architecture is technically plausible, and qualitative results illustrate useful interior-part editing capabilities.
weaknesses: Training–evaluation separation is not documented. Training includes Objaverse and PartNet assets, while principal evaluations use PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE. The paper does not describe benchmark exclusions, asset-level splits, or duplicate removal. This does not establish contamination, but leaves the central open-world generalization claim insufficiently verified.

The headline automatic-segmentation comparison substantially changes PartField by removing connectivity and replacing its clustering with K-means. Artist-provided connectivity is a legitimate input cue; its predictive power alone does not establish label leakage. Appendix Table 4 usefully supplies connectivity-enabled results, but the advantage then narrows to 81.3 versus 79.2 IoU, considerably qualifying the large-margin narrative.

Automatic evaluation selects the best ground-truth IoU across candidate masks and multiple granularities. This measures proposal coverage rather than the quality of a single automatically selected decomposition. Candidate counts are not clearly controlled, and partition quality, false-positive masks, and deployment-time granularity selection remain insufficiently evaluated.

The contribution primarily integrates established components: PartField encoders, SAM-style decoding and interaction, and frozen/trainable branches. Existing ablations support the combination but do not isolate added capacity, auxiliary attributes, or triplet loss. Claims about catastrophic forgetting and architectural scalability therefore exceed the causal evidence.

The 'native 3D' framing understates reliance on SAM-derived PartField initialization and PartField-generated pseudo-labels. Model agreement under simulated corrective clicks does not independently establish semantic annotation quality. The assertion that annotation errors are negligible lacks a human audit or quantitative quality assessment, and interior-structure advantages are demonstrated mainly qualitatively.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement: dataset manifests and release plans are unspecified, several filtering and inference thresholds are missing, and Tables 1–3 give inconsistent full-model results without explanation. Quantitative testing on generated meshes and scans, plus uncertainty estimates for smaller gains, would strengthen the evidence.

strengths: PartSAM addresses an important problem with a useful combination of interactive and automatic 3D part segmentation. The dual-branch encoder and large-scale annotation pipeline form a coherent, technically plausible system.
Interactive results are strong: single-click IoU improves from 29.4 to 56.1 on PartObjaverse-Tiny and from 35.9 to 59.5 on PartNetE, with improvements sustained across additional clicks.

The appendix provides meaningful supporting experiments, including Point-SAM retrained on the proposed data, encoder and dataset ablations, scaling curves, and additional evaluation on five 3DCoMPaT++ categories. These strengthen the evidence beyond the main benchmark comparisons.

The reported inference costs are practical, and qualitative examples demonstrate promising segmentation of occluded structures, generated meshes, and editable interior parts. Failure cases and limitations are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: Training–evaluation separation is insufficiently documented. Training includes Objaverse and PartNet assets, while central evaluations use PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE. The manuscript provides no explicit asset exclusion, deduplication, or split audit. This does not establish contamination, but leaves the central open-world generalization claims inadequately verified.

The headline automatic-segmentation comparison modifies PartField by removing connectivity and replacing its clustering with K-means, while SAMesh retains connectivity. Useful input geometry is not inherently label leakage. Appendix Table 4 partially addresses this concern: with connectivity, PartSAM scores 81.3 versus PartField's 79.2, a much smaller advantage than the main comparison suggests. Both protocols should receive equal prominence.

Automatic evaluation selects the best matching masks across multiple segmentation scales using ground truth. This measures candidate-mask coverage more directly than the quality of a single deployable decomposition. Partition consistency, redundant predictions, and uncovered regions are not adequately assessed, and candidate budgets are not clearly controlled across methods.

The annotation pipeline's semantic quality is not independently validated. Agreement with PartField pseudo-labels after simulated corrective clicks establishes reproducibility of those masks, not necessarily semantic correctness. Claims that annotation errors are negligible need a human audit or equivalent independent evidence, plus a comparison against unfiltered pseudo-labels at matched data volume.

The strongest claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Interior segmentation and robustness to generated meshes are primarily supported qualitatively. Architectural novelty is largely an integration of PartField, SAM-style decoding, and a frozen/trainable branch design; controlled ablations do not isolate auxiliary attributes, triplet loss, or increased encoder capacity. The dependence on SAM-derived initialization and PartField pseudo-labels also warrants more qualified positioning of the method as native 3D learning.

Reproducibility has unresolved gaps: exact dataset composition and filtering thresholds are missing, and Table 3 reports different full-model results from Tables 1–2 without explanation, including automatic IoU of 68.5 versus 69.5. These issues, together with the evaluation uncertainties, place an otherwise promising submission slightly below the acceptance threshold.
